objection: If Jesus is God, why did he pray to God?
answer:
Notice what the objection has to prove: not that Father and Son are personally distinct—everyone agrees on that—but that this personal distinction excludes Jesus from being fully God. John 17:3 shows the first; it doesn't show the second. The same Gospel that records Jesus praying "Father... the only true God" opens by declaring the Word was God (John 1:1) and closes with Thomas addressing the risen Jesus as "my Lord and my God" (John 20:28), a confession Jesus accepts rather than corrects. John did not think these statements contradicted each other; neither should we.

As for the prayers and "My God and your God" (John 20:17): these are exactly what we'd expect given the Incarnation. The Son, in taking true humanity, took a human nature that prays, depends, obeys, and calls the Father "My God" — because as man, He does have a God. That's not a problem for His deity; it's the necessary shape of real incarnation. If the Word truly became flesh (John 1:14), then the eternal Son now lives a genuine human life addressed toward the Father, without that human life exhausting who He is. Hebrews 1:8 shows the reverse side of this same relationship: the Father Himself addresses the Son as "O God," in direct vocative address — so within the very Godhead there is a Father who is addressed as God and a Son who is addressed as God, in distinct persons.

Finally, watch what the early Christians actually did with the "one whom the Father sent": they prayed to Him. Stephen commends his spirit to "Lord Jesus" (Acts 7:59); the Church invoked Maranatha, "Our Lord, come" (1 Corinthians 16:22); believers everywhere are described as those who call upon the name of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 1:2). If Jesus were merely an exalted agent, this would be exactly the idolatry Isaiah 45 forbids — worship rendered to any but YHWH alone. Instead, Philippians 2:9–11 has Paul deliberately apply Isaiah's language of universal worship to Jesus, and calls this the Father's glory, not a rival to it. So the "sent" language and the prayer to the Father express real, eternal personal order within the one God; they don't demote the Son from the divine identity into which He was, is, and remains fully received.

# Objection: Jesus's Prayer to God

Look, this is the hardest saying for your position. In John 17:3, Jesus himself says: "This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." He's distinguishing himself from the only true God—he's the one *sent*, not the sender. And he does this throughout the Gospels: he prays to the Father, asks the Father for things, says "My God and your God" in John 20:17. If Jesus were truly God in the fullest sense, wouldn't he be praying to himself? That makes no rational sense. The straightforward reading is that Jesus is God's unique Son, his agent and messenger—deeply exalted, yes—but not God himself. How do you explain Jesus addressing God as "you" and himself as distinct from that "only true God"?
